title: Islands that refilled
teaches: Mangrove islets, arrivals, losses and the species-area rule

blocks.text: In the shallow water of Florida Bay, off the Florida Keys, stand tiny islands made of nothing but a single clump of red mangrove: a tangle of arching roots and leaves, a dozen metres or so across, rising straight out of the sea. Each is a whole world for the insects, spiders, mites and other small animals that live in its branches. In 1966 E. O. Wilson[^wilson] of Harvard and his graduate student Daniel Simberloff picked out several of them, at distances from about 2 metres to about half a kilometre from the larger mangrove forest along the shore.

First they counted everything that lived on each islet, climbing through the branches with collecting jars, finding between about twenty and forty kinds on each. Then they hired a pest-control company to put up scaffolding over each islet, cover it with a tent, and fill the tent with poison gas, the way a house is fumigated for termites. Every insect and spider died, while the mangroves, which the gas barely harmed, stood unhurt. Then Simberloff went back, month after month, to see what came.

blocks.caption: A red mangrove islet in Florida Bay, the kind Simberloff and Wilson tented and emptied.

blocks.text: Life came back fast. Flying insects arrived first, then spiders ballooning in on silk threads, then mites riding on other animals. Within a year most of the islets held about as many kinds as before they were emptied. The islet nearest shore filled fastest. The farthest, about half a kilometre out, was still short of its old count after two years.

The kinds were not the same, though. The count came back to about where it had been, but the list was different: some species that had lived there before never returned, and others that had never been recorded there took their place. And the list kept changing after the count had settled. Species arrived, held on for a while, and died out, and others arrived. The number held steady while the members changed, like the number of guests in a hotel.

This was exactly what Wilson and the mathematical ecologist Robert MacArthur had predicted a few years before, in a theory they set out in a 1963 paper and a 1967 book, *The Theory of Island Biogeography*. Their idea was that the number of species on an island is a balance between two flows. Species arrive from the mainland, and species on the island die out. The rate of arrival falls as the island fills up, because more and more of the arrivals are kinds already there. The rate of loss rises as the island fills, because there are more species to lose and less room for each. Where the two rates meet, the number holds steady.

Two things set where they meet. Distance: a far island gets fewer arrivals. Size: a small island holds smaller populations, which die out more easily by chance, a bad year or a disease. So a big island near the mainland holds the most species, and a small one far out the fewest. It is lesson 2's bathtub again: arrivals are the tap, losses the drain, and species the water.

blocks.caption: An island emptied of insects, refilling. Each absent kind may arrive in any year, more likely on a near island; each present kind may die out, more likely on a small one. The dashed line is where arrivals balance losses. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then move the island at least 400 metres out and play 30 years

blocks.text: Simberloff and Wilson's islets did what the model does. The count rose to its old level and wobbled there, the farthest islet more slowly and to fewer, and the list kept turning over[^krakatoa].

Distance alone does not explain every island. In 1859 Alfred Russel Wallace, the naturalist who had worked out natural selection independently of Darwin, described a strange boundary in the islands of what is now Indonesia. Bali and Lombok are about 35 kilometres apart, with the same climate and similar forests. But the birds and mammals of Bali are Asian, like those of Java and Borneo, while Lombok's begin to look Australian: cockatoos and honeyeaters, and farther east, marsupials.

The explanation is the sea floor. During the ice ages, so much water was locked in ice sheets that sea level fell by over a hundred metres, and Bali, Java, Sumatra and Borneo were joined to Asia by dry land. The channel between Bali and Lombok is deep and never dried out. Animals that walk could cross the land bridges but not the strait. The line Wallace drew follows the edge of the old continental shelf. An island's history, and the barriers its colonists had to cross, matter as much as its distance on today's map.

Bigger islands hold more species, and in a strikingly regular way. In 1957 the American entomologist Philip Darlington counted the kinds of amphibians and reptiles on the islands of the West Indies, from tiny Redonda to Cuba, and found a simple rule: every tenfold increase in area roughly doubles the number of species. Ecologists write it as S = cA^z, where S is the number of species, A the area, c a number that depends on the kind of animal and the region, and z a number that sets how steeply species climb with area. Darlington's rule is z of about 0.3, since 10 to the power 0.3 is about 2.

blocks.caption: Kinds of amphibians and reptiles on seven islands of the West Indies against their area, both on scales where each step is ten times the last, from Darlington's counts as MacArthur and Wilson reprinted them. Tilt the line S = cA^z to fit.
blocks.task: Fit the line to the islands

blocks.text: The **species-area rule** holds widely: for birds on islands, for plants on mountaintops, for fish in lakes, for insects in patches of forest, though the value of z varies, from about 0.15 for areas within one stretch of mainland to 0.35 or so for true islands[^z].

blocks.title: An estimate
points: If ten times the area holds twice the species, then a hundredth of the area holds a half of a half: a quarter of the species. Cuba holds about 80 kinds of amphibians and reptiles in Darlington's table; an island a hundredth its size, about 1,100 km², should hold about 20. Montserrat, about a tenth of that again at 102 km², should hold about 10 and holds 9.

blocks.text: An island need not be surrounded by sea. A lake is an island of water in a sea of land. A mountaintop is an island of cold in a sea of warmth, which is why the zones of lesson 17, squeezed to the summits, behave like shrinking islands. A wood in farmland, a park in a city and a national park surrounded by farms and towns are all islands, with species arriving from outside and dying out within, and the same arithmetic applies. In the 1970s Jared Diamond and others began asking what island biogeography meant for nature reserves: how big they had to be, and whether one large reserve held more than several small ones of the same total area. The next lesson takes the theory to the forests being cut today.

blocks.caption: Six questions on islands
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: After Simberloff and Wilson emptied the mangrove islets, what returned within about a year on the nearer islets?
choices: About the same number of species, but not the same species
The same species as before, in the same numbers
Far more species than before, with no competitors
items.why: The count came back to near its old level while the list changed, as the arrivals-and-losses theory predicts.

items.ask: In MacArthur and Wilson's theory, why does the arrival of new species slow down as an island fills?
choices: More and more of the arrivals are kinds already there
The island gets harder to reach as it fills
Species already there drive arrivals away
items.why: Only kinds not yet present count as new. As the island fills, fewer of the mainland's kinds are missing.

items.ask: Why does a small island lose species faster than a large one?
choices: Its populations are smaller, so a bad year wipes one out more easily
Its species are mostly newer arrivals that don't fit in
Its plants can't feed as many kinds of insect
items.why: Small populations die out by chance more easily. Distance affects arrivals; size mostly affects losses.

items.ask: Bali and Lombok are 35 km apart, with similar climates, but have different mammals. Why?
choices: The strait between them is deep and stayed open when ice-age seas fell
Lombok's animals were brought by people from Australia
Bali's mammals were wiped out by a volcano and replaced
items.why: Land bridges joined Bali to Asia in the ice ages, but the deep strait never dried, so walking animals couldn't cross.

items.ask: With Darlington's rule, ten times the area holds about twice the species. About how many species would an island a hundredth the size of one with 80 hold?
items.why: A hundredth is two tenfold steps down, so halve twice: 80, 40, 20.

items.ask: Which of these behaves most like an island, in the sense of this lesson?
choices: A patch of forest surrounded by farmland
A large forest stretching unbroken for hundreds of kilometres
items.why: A patch of habitat surrounded by other land gets arrivals from outside and loses species within, just as an island does.

summary: **Simberloff and Wilson emptied mangrove islets in 1966.** Within a year most held as many kinds as before, but not the same kinds.
**An island's species are a balance of arrivals and losses.** The count settles where the two rates meet, while the list keeps changing.
**Distance sets arrivals; size sets losses.** Big islands near the mainland hold the most species.
**History matters too.** Wallace's line follows a deep strait that ice-age land bridges never crossed.
**Ten times the area holds about twice the species.** Darlington's species-area rule, S = cA^z with z near 0.3.
**Habitat patches are islands.** Lakes, mountaintops, woods in farmland and parks follow the same arithmetic.

krakatoa.title: Krakatoa
krakatoa.text: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, sterilised what was left of the island under deep ash. Within three years ferns and grasses were growing; within fifty, forest and dozens of kinds of birds. Naturalists' repeated visits made it the first island whose refilling was watched from the start.

z.title: Why z differs
z.text: Within a stretch of mainland, a small area holds many species just passing through from the surroundings, so small areas look richer and the curve is shallower. True islands have no such flow, so small ones are poorer and the curve is steeper.

wilson.title: E. O. Wilson
wilson.text: Wilson, who died in 2021, began as an ant specialist (branch N, on ants, follows his work on their trails) and went on to found island biogeography with MacArthur, sociobiology, and much of the modern argument for protecting biodiversity, the subject of the next lesson.
